analysis.title: What do the US midterms mean for Asia?
key_insights: Democrats now control both chambers of the US Congress after flipping seven Senate seats and winning their largest House majority in nearly two decades. Natixis says this limits how much President Trump can do on his own, and the net effect for Asia is positive.

Asia's three main exposures are energy imports (mostly via the Gulf), dependence on the US market for exports, and the largest stock of dollar assets outside the US, which needs an independent Fed. Natixis says all three benefit from a more constrained Trump.

Close to four-fifths of the crude and LNG trapped by the Strait of Hormuz disruption was bound for Asia. Vice President Vance has said the war cost Republicans the election, and incoming House leadership has pledged to end it. Congress cannot stop the war on its own but can make continuing it more costly.

Markets have already discounted a much lower oil risk premium before any deal is signed. Natixis names India, the Philippines, Thailand, Korea and Japan as the winners among large energy importers with external vulnerabilities.

Lower oil prices mean narrower current-account deficits, support for the rupee, the peso and the won, and more room for Asian central banks that had been pushed to hike by inflation and weaker currencies.

The Supreme Court struck down the emergency-powers tariffs in February. A Democratic Congress is unlikely to repeal presidential tariff authority but will refuse to extend temporary measures, hold hearings on price impact and push for exemptions. The main gain for Asia is a lower probability of new tariffs, not a lower average tariff.

Uncertainty, rather than the tariff level, has been holding back investment in Asia's export sector. ASEAN manufacturing hubs such as Vietnam and Malaysia, Japanese and Korean carmakers, and Chinese exporters routing through third markets should see a lower policy risk premium.

With the Senate in Democratic hands, the White House can no longer fill Fed board seats with loyalists, and removing sitting governors will be much harder. The risk of politically driven rate cuts has fallen sharply, though Natixis says it was probably always lower than the market assumed.

Asian central banks, life insurers and households are the largest foreign creditors of the US, and most of the region's trade is invoiced in dollars. Natixis calls a credible Fed the best financial stability anchor Asia can find.

AI hardware is the one area where the midterms cut the other way. New Democratic governors of Texas, Ohio and Georgia campaigned on pausing or conditioning data-centre construction over electricity bills, and AI-related stocks fell as results came in. Taiwan and Korea, whose chip, memory and server exports are priced for uninterrupted US buildouts, are the most exposed.

Natixis argues AI deployment is unlikely to hit a hard stop because AI is needed for productivity and for US strategic competition with China, and states compete for data centres for jobs, tax revenue and utility customers. Blocked projects are more likely to move to another state. For TSMC, SK Hynix and Samsung this means a longer order cycle, not the end of the AI boom.

Trump's China approach this year (Beijing summit in May, Xi Jinping state visit to Washington in September) has been transactional, and Japan has felt the cost, with Trump avoiding explicit backing for Prime Minister Takaichi in her dispute with Beijing. A Democratic Congress will scrutinise any deal trading Taiwan arms sales, export controls or US military presence for Chinese purchase commitments.

Natixis concludes the second half of Trump's term will be shaped by constraints rather than impulses: a more credible Fed, cheaper energy, fewer tariff shocks and sturdier alliances for Asia, against a slower but still intact AI investment cycle.

sector_views.sector: Energy importers in Asia (India, Philippines, Thailand, Korea, Japan)
sector_views.rationale: Lower oil risk premium narrows current-account deficits, supports the rupee, peso and won, and gives central banks room to ease.

sector_views.sector: Asia export manufacturing (ASEAN hubs, Japanese and Korean autos, Chinese exporters via third markets)
sector_views.rationale: A Democratic Congress lowers the probability of new tariffs, which reduces the policy risk premium that has held back investment.

sector_views.sector: AI hardware (Taiwan and Korea chips, memory, servers)
sector_views.rationale: Data-centre pauses in some states threaten a longer order cycle, but AI demand is expected to relocate to other states, not stop.

risk_factors: Democratic governors in Texas, Ohio and Georgia pausing or conditioning data-centre construction could delay US AI buildouts and hit Taiwan and Korea chip, memory and server exports.
Trump still defends the Gulf war and Congress cannot end it on its own, so the oil risk premium decline depends on a deal that has not been signed.
A Democratic Congress is unlikely to repeal presidential tariff authority, so tariff levels may not fall.
Less room for a grand US-China bargain.
geopolitical: Strait of Hormuz disruption has trapped close to four-fifths of crude and LNG bound for Asia, and the Republican-led war is seen as having cost the party the midterms.
Incoming House Democratic leadership has pledged to end the Gulf war, while Trump still defends it.
The Supreme Court struck down the emergency-powers tariffs in February and the administration is rebuilding the tariff wall on other legal grounds.

Trump held a Beijing summit with China in May and hosted Xi Jinping for a state visit in September, and Japan has felt the cost with Trump avoiding explicit backing for Prime Minister Takaichi in her dispute with Beijing.
A Democratic Congress is expected to scrutinise any deal that trades Taiwan arms sales, export controls or US military presence for Chinese purchase commitments.
